new_statements.translation: Ercolani: 'The tonic accent, if not indicated by special marks, always falls on the last syllable.'

'stomach'"), page break 21 falls inside the sentence exactly as the locator says. The p. 121 quote is verbatim at lines 6455-6477 ("Thus, original proparoxytones yield oxytones (> 1ζ) in varieties such as Forlivese.. southeast of the Marecchia syncope of original proparoxytones yields paroxytones…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Inherited Romance lexical stress, but confined to the last two syllables: loss of all final unstressed vowels except -a makes most words consonant-final oxytones (gat, cavàl, sumar), words in -a are paroxytone (cavala, amiga), and antepenult stress is excluded by a productive ban on proparoxytones (old proparoxytones become C-final paroxytones like fóran/sàbet via epenthesis, oxytones via syncope, or paroxytones with a paragogic vowel in San Marino); a lexical residue of vowel-final oxytones (tumarà, avnù, piò, apocopated infinitives cantê) and C-final paroxytones means position is not fully predictable from word shape, which is why the orthographies mark exactly those cases.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Michelotti marks secondary stress in transcriptions (e.g. [ˈljɛviˌto], p. xix) and reconstructs historical secondary-stress patterns (1ζ2ζζ north vs 1ζζ2ζ southeast of the Marecchia, p. 121) but states no synchronic secondary-stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Sammarinese sporadically restores etymological posttonic vowels in a few lexicalised items (sàbet, ståmmeg, Rèmmin; Vitali & Pioggia 2010: 11; Michelotti p. 122); numerals 11-16 oscillate between forms with and without paragogic vowel; proclitic words (sèmpar, tânt, zent) lose or weaken their stress onto the following word (Casadio, la Ludla sett. 2006 p. 10).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (citation forms); Michelotti notes the proparoxytone ban and the ban on heavy atonic final syllables also operate over the prosodic word verb+enclitic (pp. 204-205, 422, 447); Vitali 2008 notes long/open-mid vowels always bear word stress but can be de-stressed in the phrase.
new_statements.identity_note: Michelotti 2008 is fieldwork-based on Sammarinese (dialects of the Republic of San Marino, which he classes as 'Borderline Romagnol'), but the quoted ch. 1-2 statements are framed for the Romagnol group as a whole and explicitly contrast Central Romagnol (Forlì/Ravenna plain, the 'rf' koiné of Vitali) with Sammarinese; both fall under Glottolog roma1328 (countries IT; SM), no separate glottocode for Sammarinese known to me. Ercolani [1960] and Lapucci 1986 describe the Ravenna-Forlì plain varieties. Pesarese (Vitali & Pioggia ch. 36, also saved) is Gallo-Italic of the Marche, not Romagnol proper, and was not used.

new_statements.quote: I §7.6 p. 89: „Im Auslaut fallen sämtliche unbetonten Vokale mit Ausnahme von -a. Diese Regel gilt auch für die Proparoxytona.“ I §8.13 p. 92: „Die Mittelvokale in Proparoxytonis fallen alle, a nicht ausgenommen. Sie bleiben jedoch meist in Buchwörtern“. II §8.13 p. 205: „Wir können demnach mit Bestimmtheit sagen, daß in Proparoxytonis zuerst der Auslautvokal, später erst der Mittelvokal geschwunden ist, der Rhythmus in den mittleren und nordwestlichen romagnolischen Mundarten also ein stetig fallender war. Darauf, daß der Rhythmus von Ri. an südöstlich ein anderer war, weil der Auslautvokal einen Nebenton trug, wurde schon in 7.6 hingewiesen“
new_statements.translation: I §7.6 p. 89: 'In final position all unstressed vowels drop, with the exception of -a. This rule also holds for the proparoxytones.' I §8.13 p. 92: 'The medial vowels in proparoxytones all drop, a not excepted. They mostly remain, however, in learned words.' II §8.13 p. 205: 'We can therefore say with certainty that in proparoxytones first the final vowel and only later the medial vowel was lost, so that the rhythm in the central and north-western Romagnol dialects was a steadily falling one. That the rhythm from Rimini south-eastwards was different, because the final vowel bore a secondary stress, was already pointed out in 7.6.'
new_statements.citation: Schürr, Friedrich (1918, 1919). Romagnolische Dialektstudien. Wien: Hölder. 150 pp.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's lexical (unpredictable) reading taken from Michelotti 2008 and is in fact its historical source: Michelotti's 'apocope affects all word-final vowels except [a]' and 'all five posttonic vowels are subject to syncope in proparoxytones' restate Schürr I §7.6 and §8.13 / II §8.13 almost verbatim (Schürr: 'a nicht ausgenommen' / 'einschließlich a'). Schürr adds (i) the geographic split — the ban on proparoxytones is realised by apocope + syncope in central/NW Romagnol but in the SE (Rimini and beyond, incl. S. Marino) the final vowel of proparoxytones survives as -ə under a secondary stress with syncope of the medial; (ii) explicit secondary-stress statements (final…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Neither volume states a stress-placement rule; both are historical phonologies that presuppose the inherited Latin/Romance lexical stress and sort every word by its etymological stress class (Betonte Vokale: a) Paroxytona, b) Proparoxytona, c) Oxytona; Unbetonte Vokale: Auslaut, Nachtonvokale, Vortonvokale 'vor dem Hauptton / unter dem Nebenton / nach dem Nebenton'). What it does state: in central and NW Romagnol (Imola-Lugo-Faenza-Forlì-Ravenna-Cesena) all unstressed final vowels except -a are apocopated and all post-tonic medial vowels (including a) are syncopated, so inherited proparoxytones become monosyllables or paroxytones (e.g. Ce.PM. mangh = manico, medgh = medico); the resulting word rhythm is 'steadily falling' (main stress then no secondary prominence). In the SE (from Rimini: Ri., Ro. = Riccione, Mo., Misano, S. Marino, Pesaro, Urbino) the medial vowel is syncopated but the final vowel of proparoxytones survives as -ə because it bore a secondary stress (ˈ.ˌ 'as in French'). In word-final rising diphthong -ié the accent was retracted to -íə in the city of Cesena and the SE (II §5.162 pp. 164-165; I p. 79), while the c. 1591 Pulon Matt still rhymes with -ié stressed on the second element (I §5.162 p. 71). Stress position itself is thus lexical (inherited), with a strong tendency to eliminate antepenultimate stress by vowel deletion.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes, explicitly: II §7.6 p. 199 and §8.13 p. 205 — in the SE dialects (from Rimini south-east) the final syllable of proparoxytones 'einen Nebenton trug, also ˈ.ˌ wie im Französischen' (Meyer-Lübke, Franz. Gramm. §120), which is why final -ə is retained there; in the central and NW dialects the rhythm was 'ein einfach fallender / stetig fallender' with no secondary prominence on the final. Pretonic secondary stress is assumed in the sectioning of pretonic vowels (§8.22 'Unter dem Nebenton', §8.23 'Nach dem Nebenton'; e.g. Fa.CN. cantarin, spadarina, beccharia, I §8.22-8.23), i.e. a secondary stress on the initial syllable of longer words, in the usual Romance way; Schürr does not discuss its placement further.
new_statements.exceptions: Learned and borrowed words (Buchwörter, Lehnwörter) keep their medial vowel and remain proparoxytone (I §8.13 p. 92; II §8.13 p. 203: 'Nur in jungen Lehn- und Buchwörtern bleiben sie bewahrt'; sùbit, dùbit restored in Ra.Ga. and modern dialects after older syncopated dubt, subt in Ce.PM.); in the SE, syncope applies even in loans. Final -a is always retained. Accent retraction in word-final -ié > -íə (Ce. city, SE) and secondary stress on final -ə of proparoxytones in the SE; both are areal exceptions to the central pattern. Nachträge p. 246: the falling tone (Fallton) of the spontaneous diphthongs 'entspricht deren allgemeinen Akzentverhältnissen' and diphthongization is attributed to musical pitch movement rather than expiratory stress — a remark on the phonetic nature of the accent, not a claim that stress is absent.
new_statements.identity_note: Vol. I (1918) is a phonology of old Romagnol texts: Fa.CN. (La commedia nuova di Pier Francesco da Faenza), Ce.PM. (Pulon Matt, c. 1591, contado of Cesena left of the Savio), Ra.Ga., Ra.M., Ra.L. (Ravenna sonnets, 1709-1799). Vol. II (1919) covers living dialects recorded with the phonograph: Imola (I.), Lugo (L.), Faenza (Fa.), Forlì (Fo.), Meldola (Me.), Cesena (Ce.), Ravenna (Ra.), Castiglione di Ravenna (Ca.Ra.), Santarcangelo (SA.), Rimini (Ri.), Riccione (Ro.), Mo., Misano, and outlying points S. Marino, Pesaro, Urbino. Schürr's own dialect split is central/NW Romagnol (falling rhythm, no final secondary stress) versus the SE from Rimini (final -ə of proparoxytones under secondary stress, accent retraction -ié > -íə also in the city of Cesena).
